summary: This informational RFC gives clear definitions of active and passive performance assessment for metrics and methods. It also defines hybrid methods that mix attributes of both, and describes dimensions along which methods can be compared.

plainLanguage.summary: One way to check traffic is to send your own test car and see how it does. The other is to watch the cars already driving. This gives names to both and the mixes in between.

questions: what is hybrid type i measurement
subtitle: Precise definitions of active, passive and hybrid network measurement, and the dimensions for comparing them.

tldr.problem: The words Active and Passive have long described network performance measurement, but without precise definitions, and new methods mix both.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Active and Passive methods and metrics, adds Hybrid Type I and Type II categories, and compares methods along two dimensions: effect on the network and prior knowledge of the stream.
tldr.outcome: Measurement engineers get shared vocabulary for classifying methods such as the IPv6 PDM option or packet coloring.

facts.label: Categories
facts.value: Active, Passive, Hybrid Type I, Hybrid Type II

facts.label: Evaluation dimensions
facts.value: 2 (effect on network, a priori stream knowledge)

today: RFC 7799 is an Informational document published in May 2016, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a terminology document and defines no protocol.

sections.title: Active and Passive in Measurement
sections.content:
The terms Active and Passive have distinguished two classes of Internet performance assessment for many years; the first Passive and Active Measurement (PAM) Conference was held in 2000. In general, an Active Metric or Method depends on a dedicated measurement packet stream and observations of that stream. A Passive Metric or Method depends solely on observing one or more existing packet streams, which are present whether or not measurement takes place.

This memo gives more detailed definitions based on long usage, especially in the IETF, defines a new category for combinations, and describes dimensions for evaluating new methods. It treats Active and Passive as a continuum.
sections.plainLanguage: Active means you make your own test traffic. Passive means you only watch traffic that was going to happen anyway.

sections.title: Active Methods and Metrics
sections.content:
Active Methods generate packet streams, sometimes called synthetic streams. The packets carry fields dedicated to measurement; a sequence number is the most common, often combined with a timestamp. The Source and Destination are usually known a priori, and the stream's characteristics are known at the Source. A loading stream may be added to raise traffic, even if it is not measured.

Because they add traffic, Active Methods influence what they measure, so testers should quantify or minimize the effect. An Active Metric builds one or more aspects of Active Methods into its definition. The IETF IP performance metrics, developed under the framework in RFC 2330, are the example given: they include the source-packet stream characteristics and the Source and Destination addresses as parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: An active test is like sending your own toy car down the road with a number on it, so you know exactly which car to watch. Your car being there can slow down the others a little.

sections.title: Passive Methods and Metrics
sections.content:
Passive Methods are based solely on observing an undisturbed, unmodified packet stream. The method MUST NOT add, change or remove packets or fields, or change field values, anywhere along the path. They depend on the stream existing and being present at one or more designated Observation Points. Some collect information on all packets passing; others filter first and narrow the stream of interest.

Measuring something like latency usually needs several Observation Points, and the observed packets must carry enough information to match the same packet at each point. Sending the observations to a collector is an essential part of Passive Methods, and the traffic this generates can itself influence the network, which is true of any measurement system. Passive Metrics apply to observations of packet traffic and are assessed independently of the packets or flows, through observation alone. ITU-T Y.1540 is cited as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: A passive test is like standing at the roadside with a clipboard. You may not touch or change any car, and to time a trip you need helpers at two spots who can recognize the same car.

sections.title: Hybrid Methods
sections.content:
Hybrid Methods use a combination of Active and Passive attributes. With one stream of interest, the continuum looks like this at the Source: generating the stream is Active; augmenting or modifying it, or using methods that change how it is treated, is Hybrid Type I; only observing it is Passive. Observing an existing stream while also adding a loading stream is also Type I, since the stream is no longer solely observed.

Hybrid Type II methods use two or more different streams of interest with some mutual coordination, for example Active streams alongside undisturbed ones, to collect both kinds of metrics and allow joint analysis. The RFC expects unique hybrid metrics to emerge from Type II. Methods that combine a single Active stream with Passive observation at intermediate points are already defined as Spatial Metrics and Methods in RFC 5644.

Hybrid results may match Passive ones where packets with and without augmentation get the same "class C" treatment, and Passive results are then the Ground Truth for comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: If you stick a little flag on cars that are already driving, that is half active and half passive. Using several kinds of watching together is a second kind of mix.

sections.title: Comparing Methods and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC evaluates methods on two axes. The Y-axis is the effect of the measured stream on network conditions: how much the stream biases conditions for itself and others. The X-axis is a priori stream knowledge: how much is known about the stream in advance. Different methods can give different results on the same path at the same time. An Active throughput test adds traffic and may lower throughput for all streams, while a Passive one can err low because of host limits or private sub-networks.

Worked examples classify real proposals:

  • The IPv6 Performance and Diagnostic Measurements (PDM) option adds measurement fields to a user stream: Hybrid Type I.
  • Packet "coloring", which rewrites a field to support measurement: Hybrid Type I, with a smaller intended effect than PDM.
  • In Y.1731, Loss Measurement (LM) augments user traffic: Hybrid Type I. Synthetic Loss Measurement (SLM) and Delay Measurement (DM) inject dedicated frames: Active.

The security considerations section only refers readers to the LMAP framework (RFC 7594) for security and privacy of measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: Methods can be compared by how much they disturb traffic and how much you know about it beforehand. Active tests disturb more and know more, passive tests disturb nothing and know little.
